o: Team a is champion iff no team is stronger than it. By the transitivity guarantee, exactly one team beats everyone: its grid row contains 1 everywhere except the diagonal. In example 2, row 1 is [1,0,1] — all wins — so team 1 is champion. With n <= 100, checking row sums suffices.
k: The champion's row sums to n-1 (beats everyone).
Transitivity guarantees uniqueness, so no tie-breaking is needed.

a.i: Sum each row; the unique row equal to n-1 belongs to the champion. Equivalently, a tournament 'king' can be found by elimination, but the row sum is simplest given the guarantees.
s: For each team i, count wins grid[i][j].
Return the i whose count equals n-1.

a.i: Maintain a candidate champ; for each team j, if grid[champ][j] == 0 then j beats the candidate, so champ = j. After one pass the candidate is the champion — O(n) checks beyond reading input structure conceptually, though we still touch cells lazily.
s: For j from 1 to n-1, if grid[champ][j] == 0 set champ = j.
a.t: O(n²) worst case for cell accesses but a single logical pass.

w: Row-sum is the clearest to explain; elimination is a nice tournament-theory aside. No real pitfalls given the input guarantees — diagonal is 0 and the matrix is a valid tournament.
